name: The Goddess
summary: In Wicca, the divine feminine: the Moon, the earth, and Maiden, Mother and Crone.
body:
In Wicca the Goddess is the divine feminine, honored alongside the God. She is linked with the Moon, the earth, the sea and the turning of life.

Many practitioners see her in three faces that follow the Moon: the Maiden of the waxing moon, the Mother of the full moon and the Crone of the waning moon. Others honor her through named goddesses from many cultures.

She is often represented on the altar by a silver candle, a chalice, a moon image or a shell. Practitioners honor her at the full moon esbats and throughout the Wheel of the Year.

name: The Horned God
summary: In Wicca, the divine masculine: the Sun, the wild, the hunt and the harvest.
body:
In Wicca the God is the divine masculine, partner of the Goddess. He is often pictured with horns or antlers, as lord of animals, forests and the wild.

His story follows the Sun through the year: born at Yule, growing through spring, united with the Goddess at Beltane, giving his life in the harvest, and passing into the dark at Samhain.

He is often represented on the altar by a gold candle, a wand or antlers. Practitioners honor him at the sabbats.

name: Hecate
summary: Greek goddess of crossroads, keys, torches, the night and witchcraft.
body:
Hecate is an ancient Greek goddess of crossroads, thresholds, the night, ghosts and magic. She carries torches and keys, and offerings were once left for her where three roads meet.

Many modern witches honor her as a patron of witchcraft, a guide in dark times and a guardian of boundaries. She is linked with the dark moon.

Traditional offerings include garlic, eggs, honey and bread left at a crossroads. Keys, dogs and torches are her symbols.

name: Brigid
summary: Irish goddess and saint of the hearth, poetry, smithcraft and holy wells.
body:
Brigid is an Irish goddess of poetry, smithcraft and sacred fire, later honored as Saint Brigid of Kildare, where nuns kept a flame burning for her for centuries.

She is linked with the hearth, inspiration, craft, holy wells and the first stirrings of spring. Her festival is Imbolc, on February 1.

Traditional ways to honor her include making a woven Brigid's cross from rushes, lighting a candle, and leaving a cloth outside on Imbolc eve for her blessing.

name: Isis
summary: Egyptian goddess of magic, motherhood, protection and devotion.
body:
Isis is one of the great goddesses of ancient Egypt. In myth she gathered the scattered pieces of her husband Osiris, restored him with her magic, and protected their son Horus.

She is honored as a mistress of magic, a devoted mother and wife, and a protector. Her worship spread across the Roman world.

Her symbols include the throne headdress, wings and the tyet knot. Many modern practitioners call on her for magic, protection and the strength to rebuild after loss.

name: Freya
summary: Norse goddess of love, beauty, seiðr magic and the fallen in battle.
body:
Freya is a Norse goddess of love, beauty, gold and the magic called seiðr, a practice of trance and seeing. She drives a chariot pulled by cats and wears a famous necklace, Brísingamen.

In myth she receives half of those who fall in battle into her hall. She is also linked with the Old Norse name behind Friday in some accounts.

Modern practitioners honor her for love, self-worth, magic and courage.

name: Diana
summary: Roman goddess of the Moon, the hunt, wild places and women.
body:
Diana is the Roman goddess of the Moon, the hunt, forests and wild animals, and a protector of women. She is linked with the Greek Artemis.

She has a special place in modern witchcraft. Some traditions honor her as Queen of the Witches, and her name is used for the Goddess in some Wiccan rites.

Her festival, the Nemoralia, was held at her lake sanctuary near Rome in mid-August with torches and floating candles; many celebrate it on August 13.

name: Persephone
summary: Greek queen of the underworld and maiden of spring: cycles, return and renewal.
body:
Persephone is the Greek daughter of Demeter, carried off to the underworld by Hades. Because she ate pomegranate seeds there, she spends part of each year below as its queen and returns each spring.

Her story explains the seasons and holds both sides of life: the bright maiden of flowers and the dark queen of the dead.

She is honored at the equinoxes and in work on change, grief, returning home and finding power in hard places. The pomegranate is her symbol.

name: Cernunnos
summary: Celtic horned god of animals, forests, fertility and abundance.
body:
Cernunnos is a Celtic god known mainly from ancient images of an antlered figure seated among animals, wearing or holding a torc. His name survives on a single Roman-era stone found in Paris.

Little of his myth is known. Modern practitioners honor him as lord of wild animals, forests, fertility and the cycle of life and death, and he is often identified with the Wiccan Horned God.

Antlers, stags, serpents and torcs are his symbols.

name: Aphrodite
summary: Greek goddess of love, desire, beauty and the sea foam.
body:
Aphrodite is the Greek goddess of love, desire and beauty, said in one tale to have risen from the sea foam. The Romans knew her as Venus.

She governs attraction, pleasure, beauty and the bonds between lovers. Doves, roses, myrtle, apples and seashells are her symbols.

Modern practitioners call on her for love, self-love, confidence in the body and the pleasures of life.

name: Tonantzin
summary: Mexica "our revered mother": a title of mother goddesses honored at Tepeyac.
body:
Tonantzin means "our revered mother" in Nahuatl. In Mexica religion it was a title given to mother goddesses, and a shrine to a mother goddess stood on the hill of Tepeyac before the Spanish conquest.

After 1531 the Virgin of Guadalupe was honored on the same hill. Historians still debate how closely the two are connected, but many people today, especially in Indigenous and Chicana communities, speak of Tonantzin and Guadalupe together.

She is honored as a mother of the earth and of the people, a source of nourishment, protection and belonging.

name: Quetzalcóatl
summary: The Feathered Serpent: wind, learning, creation and the morning star.
body:
Quetzalcóatl, the Feathered Serpent, is one of the oldest and most important figures in Mesoamerican religion, honored long before the Mexica at places like Teotihuacan.

Among the Mexica he was a god of wind, learning, priesthood, the calendar and craft. In one creation story he travels to the land of the dead to bring back bones from which humans were made. He is linked with Venus as the morning star.

Modern practitioners honor him for wisdom, learning, creativity and new beginnings.

name: Tláloc
summary: Mexica god of rain, storms, lightning and the fertile earth.
body:
Tláloc is the Mexica god of rain, storms and lightning, on whom every harvest depended. He shared the top of the Templo Mayor in Tenochtitlan with Huitzilopochtli, showing how central water was.

He is shown with goggle-like rings around his eyes and fangs, and his paradise, Tlalocan, was a green land of plenty.

His rain could bring life or destroy it, so he was honored with respect. Modern practitioners call on him for rain, gardens, abundance and the power of storms.

name: Mictecacíhuatl
summary: Mexica Lady of the Dead, queen of Mictlán and guardian of bones.
body:
Mictecacíhuatl is the Mexica Lady of the Dead, who ruled Mictlán, the land of the dead, with Mictlantecuhtli. She was said to guard the bones of the dead.

Ancient festivals for the dead were held in her honor, and many people today connect her with the roots of Día de Muertos. Modern images of La Catrina are sometimes linked to her, though La Catrina herself began as a twentieth-century print.

She is honored in remembrance of the dead, ancestor work and acceptance of life's end.

name: Chalchiuhtlicue
summary: Mexica "she of the jade skirt": rivers, lakes, springs and newborns.
body:
Chalchiuhtlicue, "she of the jade skirt", is the Mexica goddess of rivers, lakes, springs and fresh water, and the partner or sister of Tláloc.

She watched over water journeys and over newborns, who were washed in her name. She is shown wearing a green or jade skirt with water flowing from it.

Modern practitioners honor her for cleansing, fresh starts, flowing emotion and blessing of water.

name: Xochiquetzal
summary: Mexica goddess of flowers, beauty, love, art and weaving.
body:
Xochiquetzal, "precious flower", is the Mexica goddess of flowers, beauty, love, pleasure and the arts, especially weaving and embroidery. Artisans honored her as their patron.

She is shown young and lovely, surrounded by flowers, butterflies and birds, especially the marigold.

Modern practitioners call on her for love, beauty, creativity, craftwork and the pleasures of life.
